meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If a man does not know to what port he is sailing, no wind is favorable'?
meta.ogDescription: Not JFK. The line is Seneca the Younger's (Moral Letters, Letter 71). Kennedy quoted it in 1960 and credited Socrates.

answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — actually Seneca the Younger
answer.authorDates: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher & statesman
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Seneca’s, from his Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter 71: “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est.” John F. Kennedy did use this exact English wording in a 1960 campaign speech in Raleigh ↗ — but he attributed it to Socrates, not himself, and it is neither Kennedy’s nor Socrates’s line. Quote Investigator ↗ documents the ancient Seneca origin.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est.”
John F. Kennedy, Raleigh speech, 17 Sept 1960 (who credited Socrates)

source.excerpt: “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est.” — rendered in the Loeb Classical Library as “When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.” Seneca is urging Lucilius that virtue requires a fixed goal: without knowing where you are headed, no favourable circumstance can help you get there.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying to Seneca the Younger’s Epistolae, Letter LXXI, section 3, giving the Latin “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est” and documented English translations from 1881, 1920 and 1988.
The exact English wording appears in Kennedy’s 17 September 1960 speech at the Raleigh Coliseum ↗, where he introduces it as a line from Socrates.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Kennedy’s 1960 remarks with an editorial note that the saying actually originates with Seneca, citing the Loeb Latin text and translations of Epistle LXXI.
source.excerptNote: The crisp modern wording — “to what port he is sailing … no wind is favorable” — is the phrasing John F. Kennedy used in 1960; older published translations say “harbour” and “making for.”

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: You Must Know Your Destination Port

source.rightsNote: The source is Seneca’s Epistulae Morales (1st century AD), long in the public domain, as are the standard 19th- and early-20th-century English translations (e.g. the 1881 “harbour” rendering). The specific popular wording is a close 20th-century variant of that public-domain text.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.heading: About Seneca the Younger
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist & statesman
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher, tragedian, and statesman who served as tutor and adviser to the emperor Nero. His Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium — 124 letters on how to live well — are among the most quoted works of Stoic thought, and the image of needing a known destination before any wind can help comes from Letter 71.

misattribution.heading: How this got pinned on the wrong people
misattribution.intro: This is a rare quote with a documented double misattribution: it is credited to Kennedy because he said it, and Kennedy himself credited the wrong ancient.

items.why: The line is Seneca's, from Epistulae Morales, Letter 71: “Ignoranti quem portum petat, nullus suus ventus est,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
Kennedy quoted the line in his 1960 Raleigh speech ↗, which is why it circulates under his name — but he was quoting, not coining, it.
In that speech Kennedy introduced the line as Socrates's; there is no basis for a Socratic source, and the saying belongs to the Roman Stoic Seneca, per Wikiquote ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording people share is Kennedy's 1960 phrasing, but the thought is Seneca's — and it is neither Kennedy's nor Socrates's, as Quote Investigator ↗ shows.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Seneca's point in Letter 71 is that effort is worthless without a fixed goal: the sailor who does not know his harbour cannot call any wind lucky. It is a compact Stoic argument that virtue requires a settled sense of purpose.
Kennedy borrowed exactly that image in 1960 to argue that America needed direction, not just energy — which is how a first-century Roman aphorism became a mid-century American campaign line.
